note: A shared, deterministic driver (cmd/retentionbench) drove two systems on the same machine, same device, same container caps: OpenZFS with a read-only snapshot after every epoch, and OrFS-GO, which retains every committed transition in its authoritative log with no extra snapshots. This receipt is data, not a leaderboard: rows are keyed by {system, kind, state, epoch, writers, readers, block_size} and are never ranked across incomparable coordinates. Read the comparability block before drawing any conclusion.
method: One defined, bounded epoch workload (append 4 KiB records with write(2)+fsync(2) per record) drives both systems. The OpenZFS arm takes a read-only snapshot after every epoch, so every committed state is retained; the OrFS-GO arm takes no snapshots, because it retains every committed transition in its authoritative log. Reads are block-aligned uniform random preads of the current state and of each retained snapshot. Space is accounted from `zfs list -o used,referenced,logicalused,logicalreferenced` and from the authoritative bytes of the OrFS volume. Latencies are exact observed samples.

container.comparator_filesystem: OpenZFS (real out-of-tree kernel module) inside a KVM micro-VM guest

comparability.question: Can a system retain every committed historical transition while achieving comparable tail latency, throughput and physical-space economics?

workload.append_durability: write(2)+fsync(2) per record (one durability barrier per record)

OpenZFS.retention: read-only snapshot after every epoch (zfs snapshot)

OrFS-GO.retention: every committed transition retained in the authoritative log (or.log); no snapshot step

comparable_axes: current-state append: the same defined epoch (one write(2)+fsync(2) per record), both systems inside the same KVM guest on the same virtual disk, measured at the syscall level.
current-state read: block-aligned uniform-random pread of the current committed state; OrFS-GO adds its FUSE round trip inside the guest.

physical vs logical bytes: retained physical bytes per logical byte. OpenZFS physical is the zfs list -o used figure of the dataset/snapshot; OrFS-GO physical is the authoritative or.log bytes (the same computation as the Btrfs court).
not_comparable: historical-state read: OpenZFS serves it from a snapshot (its .zfs/snapshot/<name> path); OrFS-GO does not serve named historical roots in this build (docs/LIMITATIONS.md), so this axis is OpenZFS-only. The OrFS-GO current-state read serves the newest committed bytes.
snapshot-creation cost: OrFS-GO has no snapshot step; it retains every committed transition at append time. The OpenZFS snapshot-creation row has no OrFS-GO counterpart.

snapshot extent sharing: OpenZFS snapshots share unchanged blocks copy-on-write, so a retained snapshot's used figure can be near zero. OrFS-GO's retained bytes are its appended log, which never shares extents; both are measured but are not the same computation.

read latency is a native-vs-FUSE comparison inside one guest: the OpenZFS read is a native guest filesystem read served from the guest page cache, while the OrFS-GO read is a FUSE request plus a daemon pread inside that same guest. The OpenZFS read IOPS therefore does not rank the OrFS-GO read.
differences: The comparator is measured inside a KVM micro-VM (a guest Ubuntu kernel with its own OpenZFS module), not in the container: absolute latencies include nested-virtualisation and virtio-disk cost. The OrFS-GO arm is measured in the SAME guest, so the two systems share that overhead and the comparison between them is apples-to-apples; the numbers are NOT comparable to the container-only Btrfs court (evidence/retention-btrfs.json).
The host kernel still has no ZFS module; OpenZFS here is the guest's module, loaded inside the guest only. The host is never modified.
The guest's ZFS ARC is bounded (zfs_arc_max) so the small VM cannot spend its RAM on cache.
Host-level variance (the guest's page cache, the host scheduler, the backing device's write cache) is not controlled beyond the shared container; run-to-run variance is expected and unquantified.
comparability.note: Both systems ran inside ONE KVM micro-VM: OpenZFS (the guest kernel's out-of-tree module) snapped read-only after every epoch, and OrFS-GO retained every committed transition in its log. The receipt is data, not a leaderboard. A lost arm inside the VM FAILs the court.

space.note: PhysicalBytes (UsedBytes) is the space the dataset and all its snapshots occupy including CoW metadata (from `zfs list -o used`); ReferencedBytes (referenced) is the logical bytes this dataset/snapshot references; LogicalUsedBytes/LogicalReferencedBytes are the compression-aware logical figures. For a snapshot, `used` is the space that would be freed by destroying it, so it is that retained state's uniquely-retained bytes.

notes: Every row is one bounded arm of cmd/retentionbench against a directory on this machine.
Read the comparability block before comparing any two rows; a row that could not be measured the same way is recorded as a caveat, not a pass or a parity claim.
The receipt deliberately carries no ranking: two rows are comparable only at the same {kind, state, epoch, writers, readers, block_size} and under the listed configuration differences.

OpenZFS retains historical states as read-only snapshots; OrFS-GO retains them in its authoritative log and does not serve named historical roots in this build, so the historical-state read axis is OpenZFS-only (recorded as not comparable).
